lessons.title: REITs: Buying Rental Yield Without Buying a Building

children.text: In Chapter 2, commercial property looked attractive on yield but came with real problems: tickets of ₹1.5 crore or more, a single tenant who could leave, vacancies that could last a year, and a buyer pool so thin that selling could take months. Now imagine owning a slice of dozens of Grade A office parks leased to hundreds of companies, starting with a few thousand rupees, collecting rent every quarter, and selling any working day on NSE or BSE through the same Zerodha account you use for shares. That is what a REIT offers. By the end of this lesson you will understand how Indian REITs work, how to measure their yield and value, how they are taxed, and when a REIT is a better way to buy rental income than buying a building yourself.

body.text: A REIT turns large, rent-producing commercial property into small, listed units. You give up control and accept daily price swings, and in return you get diversified rental income, professional management and the ability to sell in seconds.

children.text: What a REIT Is

markDefs.definition: Real Estate Investment Trust: a SEBI-regulated trust that owns income-producing real estate, mostly completed and leased, and passes most of its cash flow to unitholders.
The cash a REIT has available to distribute after operating costs, interest and other obligations, as defined under SEBI's REIT regulations.

children.text: A
REIT

is a trust that owns office parks, malls or other commercial property, usually through subsidiary companies. It collects rent from tenants, pays running costs and interest, and distributes most of what is left as
net distributable cash flow
to investors, who hold units listed on the stock exchanges. REITs in India are governed by the SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014.

stats.label: Minimum payout
stats.context: Of net distributable cash flows, paid at least half-yearly

stats.label: Borrowing cap
stats.context: Of asset value, with extra conditions above 25%

stats.label: Independent valuation
stats.context: By a registered valuer, with NAV disclosed to investors

body.text: The 80% and 90% rules are what make a REIT a rental yield product. Most of its assets must already be built and leased, so you are not betting on a developer finishing a project. And most of its cash must be paid out, so the rent actually reaches you instead of being retained.

children.text: Measuring a REIT's Yield and Return

markDefs.definition: The total distributions paid per unit over the last year, divided by the current unit price. A REIT's equivalent of rental yield.

children.text: The REIT version of rental yield is the
distribution yield
. Because the unit price moves every day, the yield you lock in depends on the price you buy at, just as a flat's yield depends on what you pay for it.

body.latex: \text{Distribution Yield} = \frac{\text{Distributions per Unit, Last 12 Months}}{\text{Current Unit Price}} \qquad \text{Total Return} = \frac{\text{Distributions} + (\text{End Price} - \text{Start Price})}{\text{Start Price}}
body.caption: Exactly the two engines from Chapter 1: income plus price change.

children.text: Say an office REIT trades at ₹380 a unit and paid ₹24 in distributions over the past year. Its distribution yield is ₹24 ÷ ₹380 = 6.32%. If the unit price ends the next year at ₹395 and distributions stay at ₹24, the total return is (₹24 + ₹15) ÷ ₹380 = 10.26%.

body.title: Calculate a distribution yield
body.prompt: A REIT's units trade at ₹345 on NSE. Over the last four quarters, it has distributed a total of ₹22.50 per unit. What is its distribution yield? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Distribution yield = ₹22.50 ÷ ₹345 × 100 = 6.52%. Compare that with the 2.5% to 3.5% net yield of a typical flat, but remember the REIT's unit price can fall as well as rise.

markDefs.definition: Net asset value per unit: the independently valued properties plus other assets, minus debt and liabilities, divided by the number of units.

children.text: REITs also disclose
NAV per unit
, based on independent valuations. Comparing the market price with NAV tells you whether the market is valuing the buildings above or below what valuers think they are worth.

body.latex: \text{Premium or Discount to NAV} = \left(\frac{\text{Unit Price}}{\text{NAV per Unit}} - 1\right) \times 100
body.caption: A unit price of ₹380 against a NAV of ₹420 is a discount of about 9.5%.

body.title: Reading a NAV discount
body.question: An office REIT trades at a 10% discount to its NAV per unit. Which interpretation is most reasonable?
options: The REIT's buildings are definitely worth 10% more than you are paying, so it is a guaranteed bargain
The market is pricing the portfolio below the valuers' estimate, perhaps because it expects higher interest rates, vacancies or weaker rents; investigate why before assuming a bargain
The REIT must be about to cut its distributions
NAV discounts do not matter for listed REITs
body.explanation: A discount can signal value, but it can also reflect the market's view that valuations are too optimistic, interest rates will stay high, or some tenants may leave. Check occupancy, lease expiries, leverage and the distribution trend before reading a discount as a bargain.

children.text: You can estimate the cap rate the stock market is applying to a REIT's buildings. Add the REIT's market capitalisation to its net debt to get the implied value of the whole property portfolio, then divide the portfolio's annual net operating income by that figure.

content.caption: Example: NOI of ₹3,900 crore ÷ (₹36,000 crore + ₹16,000 crore) = 7.5%.

children.text: If similar office buildings sell privately at a 7% cap rate but the stock market is implying 7.5%, the REIT is priced more cheaply than the private market. That gap is the same idea as a NAV discount, seen through the cap rate tool from Chapter 4.
REIT vs Owning a Commercial Unit Yourself

cells: The price of a single unit, often a few hundred rupees
Stamp duty, registration and brokerage, often around 7%
Hundreds, across many buildings and cities
You handle tenants, repairs and paperwork
Visible daily and can swing with markets and interest rates
Hidden, because nobody quotes a price daily
None over buildings, tenants or leverage
The REIT borrows, within SEBI's cap

body.text: Daily prices make REITs look riskier than a building you own, but that is partly an illusion. A physical office unit also changes value when interest rates rise or tenants leave; you just do not see a quote every morning. What REITs add is visibility and the temptation to sell in a panic. If you buy a REIT for rental income, judge it on distributions, occupancy and lease quality, not on last week's price.

children.text: How REIT Income Is Taxed

A REIT distribution is not one kind of income. Because REITs usually own buildings through subsidiary companies, what reaches you is typically a mix of interest, dividends, repayment of debt and sometimes rental income, and each part can be taxed differently. Every REIT publishes the break-up of each distribution. Here is an illustrative split.

body.title: An illustrative REIT distribution of ₹6 per unit, by component (₹)

children.text: Interest:
generally taxable at your slab rate.
Dividend:
its treatment depends on the tax regime chosen by the REIT's underlying companies, so it can be exempt or taxable in your hands.
Repayment of debt and other components:
rules for these have changed in recent budgets and can affect both current tax and your cost for capital gains.
Selling units:
gains on listed REIT units are taxed as capital gains, with a much shorter long-term holding period than physical property.

body.text: Compared with the rent from a flat or shop, which is fully taxed at your slab rate after a 30% deduction, part of a REIT distribution may be taxed lightly or not at all in the year received. Always check the component split in the REIT's distribution statement and confirm the current treatment with a chartered accountant, because REIT tax rules have been revised several times.

body.title: The payout rule
body.textWithBlank: SEBI requires a REIT to distribute at least ___% of its net distributable cash flows to unitholders.
body.explanation: The 90% payout rule, together with the rule that at least 80% of assets must be completed and rent-generating, is what makes REITs a rental income product rather than a development bet.

body.title: A ₹25 lakh shop or a basket of REITs?
body.scenario: Pooja Deshmukh, a 44-year-old school principal in Nashik, has ₹25 lakh to put into rental income. Option A: a small ground-floor shop on College Road for ₹25 lakh, plus about ₹1.75 lakh in stamp duty and registration, currently let at ₹14,000 a month. Pooja expects about one vacant month a year on average and ₹20,000 a year in owner's costs. Option B: split the ₹25 lakh across listed REITs with an average distribution yield of about 6.3%.
body.prompt: Compare the net income from each option, then weigh the non-financial trade-offs. Which fits better, and what should Pooja check?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Shop: potential rent ₹14,000 × 12 = ₹1,68,000. Minus one vacant month (₹14,000) and ₹20,000 of costs = ₹1,34,000. On ₹26.75 lakh all-in, the net yield is about 5.0%.
2. REITs: ₹25 lakh × 6.3% = about ₹1,57,500 a year, with negligible buying costs, so the income yield is about 6.3% on the money invested.
3. Beyond yield: the shop depends on one tenant, may take months to re-let or sell, and gives Pooja control and a physical asset. The REITs spread risk across hundreds of tenants and can be sold any trading day, but their unit prices will move with markets and interest rates, and Pooja has no say in how the buildings are run.
4. Tax: rent from the shop is taxed at Pooja's slab rate after the 30% deduction. Part of the REIT distributions may be taxed differently depending on their components.
5. Fit: for someone seeking steady income without landlord work, with only ₹25 lakh, the REIT route gives higher income, diversification and liquidity. The shop makes sense mainly if Pooja values control, has a strong long-term tenant and a location likely to appreciate.
6. Checks for REITs: occupancy, weighted average lease expiry, tenant concentration, borrowing level, distribution history and component split, and price relative to NAV. For the shop: the lease deed, tenant reliability, comparable rents on College Road and resale demand.

body.title: Evaluate a REIT before you buy
steps: Check occupancy and committed occupancy across the portfolio.
Check the weighted average lease expiry and how much rent comes up for renewal in the next two years.
Look at tenant concentration: how much rent comes from the top ten tenants and which sectors they are in.
Compare borrowings with asset value against SEBI's 49% cap and the REIT's own targets.
Review distribution history and the interest, dividend and other component split.
Compare the unit price with the latest NAV per unit.
Understand the sponsor, the pipeline of future acquisitions and exposure to rising interest rates.

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Search a REIT by name to see its price history, financials and filings in one place, alongside the investor presentations published on the REIT's own website and on NSE and BSE.

cards.definition: A SEBI-regulated trust that owns mostly completed, income-producing property and distributes most of its cash flow to unitholders.
REITs must distribute at least 90% of net distributable cash flows.
At least 80% of a REIT's value must be in completed, rent-generating properties.
Distributions per unit over the last year divided by the current unit price.
Independently valued assets minus liabilities, divided by units outstanding.
How far the market price sits above or below NAV per unit.
A Small and Medium REIT under SEBI's 2024 framework for smaller property pools, with a higher minimum investment.

points: A REIT owns mostly completed, leased commercial property and must distribute at least 90% of its net distributable cash flows.
Indian listed REITs include office-focused Embassy, Mindspace and Brookfield, and retail-focused Nexus Select.
Distribution yield = distributions per unit over 12 months ÷ unit price; total return adds price change, just like property.
Compare price with NAV per unit, and remember a discount needs an explanation before it counts as value.
REITs offer small tickets, diversification, professional management and liquidity, in exchange for no control and visible price swings.
Distributions are a mix of components taxed differently, so read each REIT's distribution break-up.
For modest sums aimed at rental income, a basket of REITs often beats a single small commercial unit on yield, risk and liquidity.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice, and no REIT named here is a recommendation. Unit prices, distributions, yields and NAV figures used are illustrative. REIT regulations and tax rules change, and REIT units can fall in value, so read each REIT's offer documents and disclosures and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a chartered accountant before investing.
